goal: Choose an authentication state strategy for admin-panel so the internal team can sign in securely while matching the app's current single-origin, server-rendered design.
question: Which authentication state strategy should admin-panel use for managing sign-in state?
known_constraints: Five-person internal team; small, known user base
Single-origin, server-rendered app with no external API consumers today
A mobile app is only a roadmap possibility; nothing has been decided
The codebase is Python standard library only with no third-party dependencies
No authentication exists yet; the strategy must be introduced from scratch

environment.deployment: single server, single origin, server-rendered HTML
environment.existing_auth: none implemented; placeholder sign-in form in static markup only

evidence: README.md: 'An internal admin panel for a five-person team. The app is server-rendered by its own web server and served from a single origin. There are no external API consumers today. The product roadmap mentions a possible mobile app, but nothing has been decided.' (Gloss: same-origin server-rendered internal tool; no external API clients; mobile app undecided.)
app.py: the server is built on Python's http.server with no web framework and no third-party dependencies; it serves a single GET page and binds to 127.0.0.1:8080.
app.py: the served page contains a placeholder sign-in form, but there is no login handling, session store, token issuance, or user-account code anywhere in the repository.
Repository: no configuration files, package manifests, or dependency locks exist, confirming the stdlib-only, zero-dependency state described in app.py.

alternatives.name: Server-Side Session Cookie
alternatives.description: Authenticate at login, store a session record server-side, and set an opaque random session ID in an HttpOnly SameSite cookie that is validated against the store on each request.
advantages: The session ID is opaque and HttpOnly, so it is not readable by client-side script
Logout and account disable take effect immediately by deleting the server-side session record
Matches the current same-origin, server-rendered, five-user internal app without unused machinery
Can be implemented with Python standard library primitives (e.g., the secrets module) given the zero-dependency codebase
disadvantages: Requires a session store (for example, SQLite or an in-memory map) that must persist across restarts or be regenerated
Non-browser clients would need a separate auth mechanism or a token-issuance path added later
assumptions: All current traffic is same-origin browser traffic
Operating a small session store is acceptable overhead

alternatives.name: JWT in HttpOnly Cookie
alternatives.description: Issue a signed JWT at login, return it in an HttpOnly SameSite cookie, and validate the signature on each request without server-side session state.
advantages: Stateless validation, so no session store to operate
Cookie transport keeps the token out of reach of client-side script
The token format is consumable by future non-browser clients if the roadmap item materializes
disadvantages: Revocation before expiry requires a denylist, which reintroduces server-side state
Requires signing-key management plus either a JWT library or custom signing code
Token expiry and refresh logic adds complexity for an internal five-user tool
assumptions: A signing secret can be securely stored and rotated
Short token lifetimes or a denylist are acceptable for the revocation needs of an admin panel

alternatives.name: JWT Bearer Token in Header
alternatives.description: Issue a signed JWT at login, keep it in browser storage, and send it as an Authorization: Bearer header on each request.
advantages: Stateless validation with no session store
The pattern transfers directly to mobile apps or external API clients
Decouples authentication from cookie handling and CSRF concerns
disadvantages: The token is accessible to client-side script, increasing theft exposure under cross-site scripting
No immediate revocation without a denylist
The CSRF-free property is unused today because all clients are same-origin browser pages
assumptions: Cross-site scripting risk can be adequately managed by the frontend
Future non-browser clients are likely enough to justify client-side token storage now

criteria.name: Requirement fit
rubric: Mismatched for a same-origin, server-rendered internal app
Workable but carries machinery the current app does not use
Good fit for the current app shape
Excellent fit for a same-origin, server-rendered internal app

criteria.name: Security posture
rubric: Sign-in state is readable by client-side script and hard to revoke
Sign-in state is shielded from script but hard to revoke
Sign-in state is shielded from script and immediately revocable

criteria.name: Implementation complexity
rubric: High: requires new dependencies or custom signing/crypto code
Medium: moderate state or token handling code
Low: minimal code with standard library primitives

criteria.name: Revocability
rubric: Sign-in state stays valid until token expiry with no way to revoke
Revocation possible only with extra bookkeeping such as a denylist
Immediate revocation by deleting server-side state

criteria.name: Future flexibility
rubric: Requires a separate auth mechanism for non-browser clients
Adaptable to non-browser clients with additional work
Directly reusable by non-browser clients as-is

criteria.name: Operational cost
rubric: Highest ongoing burden (stateful store to run, or key management plus rotation)
